contributions.headingText: VIPoma is a functioning well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm (NEN) composed of tumour cells with uncontrolled secretion of VIP, causing the syndrome of watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome, also called Verner–Morrison syndrome). A minority of VIPomas (typically occurring in children) are neurogenic tumours arising in the sympathetic paraganglia and adrenal glands.
2C10.1 & XH8LS0 Neuroendocrine neoplasms of pancreas & VIPoma, malignant
Not recommended: diarrhoeagenic tumour of the pancreas; islet cell tumour with watery diarrhoea.

Approximately 75–90% of VIPomas are located in the pancreas, and 10–25% outside the pancreas {10089056; 26742109}. Within the pancreas, the most common tumour location is the tail, with 70% in the body or tail and 30% in the head {9854582; 17510774; 10089056}. Most of the extrapancreatic VIPomas belong to the group of neurogenic neoplasms occurring in the adrenal glands, retroperitoneum, and mediastinum, such as phaeochromocytoma, ganglioneuroma, and ganglioneuroblastoma {3035922; 10089056}.

The key clinical features of WDHA syndrome are large-volume secretory diarrhoea (usually > 1 L of stool per day) that persists with fasting, hypokalaemia, hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria, and acidosis. Other common clinical presentations are weight loss, hypercalcaemia, glucose intolerance, and flushing {10089056; 9854582; 3035922}. The diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating high plasma VIP levels, usually > 80 pmol/L for the full syndrome. CT, MRI, EUS, MRI, octreoscan, and 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT can be used to detect primary and metastatic VIPomas {9854582; 20664472}. The radiographical appearance is similar to that of other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (PanNETs).

Pancreatic VIPoma is very rare, accounting for only 0.6–1.5% of all pancreatic NENs (PanNENs) {24121170; 24499825} and approximately 2–6% of functioning tumours {24499825; 26704781}. The incidence is 0.05–0.2 cases per 1 million person-years {26742109}.
There are no known etiological factors. Approximately 10% of pancreatic VIPomas are seen in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 {10089056; 9854582}.

Pancreatic VIPomas originate from non-β islet cells of the pancreas that produce VIP {13571250}. These tumours can produce excessive amounts of VIP, which causes intestinal secretion by activating G protein–coupled receptors on the intestinal epithelial cells, leading to watery diarrhoea and consequently dehydration and electrolyte imbalance {181379; 8103215}.

Somatic mutations in MEN1 are found in some sporadic pancreatic VIPomas. However, VHL, PTEN, or SMAD4 (DPC4) mutations have also been found {11523053; 10327057}. Chromosomal gains/losses in pancreatic VIPoma, detected by comparative genomic hybridization, are frequently aberrations of 11q, Xq, and Y {10595906}. Allelic losses of 3p and 6q in the tumours, found by loss-of-heterozygosity analysis, may be involved in tumour progression {11523053; 11395364}.
Pancreatic VIPomas are usually solitary, well circumscribed, and large (mean size: 4.5–5.3 cm) {2839087; 17510774; 10089056}.

The histopathology of pancreatic VIPomas resembles that of other well-differentiated PanNETs. The tumour cells are arranged in a solid, trabecular, or tubuloacinar pattern {2839087}. Mitoses are generally rare (< 2 mitoses/mm2), even in tumours with metastases {10089056; 24121170}. Most cases are either G1 or G2 {24121170}. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion is common {10089056}. Tumour cells express synaptophysin, chromogranin A, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CK8/18, CK19, PDX1, and SSTR2A. In some cases, low-molecular-weight cytokeratin is expressed as perinuclear dots. In most pancreatic VIPomas, VIP-immunoreactive cells are scattered. In addition, PP is frequently expressed in tumour cells {2839087}.

The tumour cells generally have modest amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland nuclei without prominent nucleoli. Like other PanNETs, VIPomas can display focal or extensive oncocytic or clear-cell changes {2839087}.

The staging of pancreatic VIPomas, like that of all PanNENs, follows the eighth editions (2017) of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification [[Brierly JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley Blackwell; 2017.]] and the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) cancer staging manual [[Amin MB, Edge S, Greene F, et al., editors. AJCC cancer staging manual. 8th ed. New York (NY): Springer; 2017.]] {28752469}, which rely on macroscopic assessment of site, tumour size, and metastases. This approach largely corresponds to that of the European Neuroendocrine Tumor Society (ENETS) classification {22525418}. The staging of well-differentiated PanNENs is presented in section Chapter 1.

Tumour grade (determined by Ki-67 proliferation index and mitotic count) and tumour stage are the two main prognostic factors. Approximately 50–80% of cases present with distant metastases at diagnosis, mostly in the liver {10089056; 3035922; 9854582}. Postoperative 5-year survival rates are 60% and 94%, respectively, for patients with and without metastasis {10089056}.
